claim: Ageing is a progressive decline of intrinsic physiological functions.
source: Ageing is a progressive decline of intrinsic physiological functions.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract as established knowledge about ageing.

claim: Mitochondrial function and ultrastructure are maintained in mouse heart during ageing.
source: Mitochondrial function and ultrastructure are maintained in mouse heart, whereas subpopulations of mitochondria from mouse liver show age-related changes in membrane morphology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from respirometry and electron cryo-tomography presented in the manuscript.

claim: Subpopulations of mitochondria from mouse liver show age-related changes in membrane morphology.
source: Mitochondrial function and ultrastructure are maintained in mouse heart, whereas subpopulations of mitochondria from mouse liver show age-related changes in membrane morphology.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data showing central voids in aged liver mitochondria.

claim: Subpopulations of mitochondria from young and old mouse kidney resemble those described for apoptosis.
source: Subpopulations of mitochondria from young and old mouse kidney resemble those described for apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data and references to apoptotic mitochondrial morphology.

claim: In aged flies, respiratory activity is compromised.
source: In aged flies, respiratory activity is compromised and the production of peroxide radicals is increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry measurements showing decreased oxygen consumption in old flies.

claim: In aged flies, the production of peroxide radicals is increased.
source: In aged flies, respiratory activity is compromised and the production of peroxide radicals is increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of peroxide yield in old fly mitochondria.

claim: In about 50% of mitochondria from old flies, the inner membrane organization breaks down.
source: In about 50% of mitochondria from old flies, the inner membrane organization breaks down.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data showing various abnormal inner membrane morphologies.

claim: There is a clear link between inner membrane architecture and functional decline in aged flies.
source: This establishes a clear link between inner membrane architecture and functional decline.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between structural changes observed by cryo-ET and functional decline measured by respirometry.

claim: Mitochondria are affected by ageing to very different extents depending on the organism.
source: Mitochondria were affected by ageing to very different extents, depending on the organism and possibly on the degree to which tissues within the same organism are protected against mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from mouse and Drosophila showing different patterns of age-related changes.

claim: Mitochondria are affected by ageing to very different extents depending on the tissue within the same organism.
source: Mitochondria were affected by ageing to very different extents, depending on the organism and possibly on the degree to which tissues within the same organism are protected against mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from mouse heart, liver, and kidney showing different patterns of age-related changes.

claim: Mitochondria produce most of the ATP in non-photosynthetic eukaryotes.
source: Mitochondria produce most of the ATP in non-photosynthetic eukaryotes, providing the energy to drive a multitude of cellular processes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: The mitochondrial genome in humans and flies encodes 13 hydrophobic subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation system.
source: In addition to a multitude of soluble enzymes and ribosomes, the matrix houses the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA), which in humans and flies encodes 13 hydrophobic subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial genetics.

claim: Nearly all mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported into the different mitochondrial compartments by a set of protein translocases.
source: Thus nearly all mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported into the different mitochondrial compartments by a set of protein translocases (Pfanner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs mostly, if not entirely, in the deeply invaginated cristae of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs mostly, if not entirely, in the deeply invaginated cristae of the inner mitochondrial membrane (Gilkerson et al., 2003; Vogel et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ATP synthase forms long rows of dimers at the tightly curved cristae ridges.
source: The ATP synthase forms long rows of dimers at the tightly curved cristae ridges, while the respiratory chain complexes are confined to the remaining membrane regions (Davies et al., 2012, 2011; Paumard et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Respiratory chain complexes are confined to the remaining membrane regions outside cristae ridges.
source: The ATP synthase forms long rows of dimers at the tightly curved cristae ridges, while the respiratory chain complexes are confined to the remaining membrane regions (Davies et al., 2012, 2011; Paumard et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Ageing has long been linked to mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Ageing has long been linked to mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the relationship between ageing and mitochondria.

claim: Harman postulated that ageing results from the accumulation of molecular damage caused by oxygen radicals.
source: More than 50 years ago, Harman postulated that ageing results from the accumulation of molecular damage caused by oxygen radicals, often called reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Harman, 1956).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harman's original work.

claim: Oxygen radicals are side products of electron transfer reactions in respiratory chain complexes I and III.
source: Oxygen radicals are side products of electron transfer reactions in respiratory chain complexes I and III (Dröse and Brandt, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The mitochondrial DNA mutator mouse model has provided experimental evidence of a causative link between mtDNA mutations and an ageing phenotype in mammals.
source: The mitochondrial DNA mutator mouse model has provided experimental evidence of a causative link between mtDNA mutations and an ageing phenotype in mammals (Trifunovic et al., 2004), although mitochondrial defects in this model were found not to be associated with an increase in ROS production (Trifunovic et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the mutator mouse model.

claim: Mitochondrial defects in the mutator mouse model were found not to be associated with an increase in ROS production.
source: The mitochondrial DNA mutator mouse model has provided experimental evidence of a causative link between mtDNA mutations and an ageing phenotype in mammals (Trifunovic et al., 2004), although mitochondrial defects in this model were found not to be associated with an increase in ROS production (Trifunovic et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In C. elegans, moderately elevated levels of ROS increase lifespan.
source: For example, in some model organisms, such as the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, moderately elevated levels of ROS, induced either chemically or through genetically engineered defects in the respiratory chain, actually increase lifespan (Heidler et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2010; Yang and Hekimi, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on C. elegans.

claim: In C. elegans, removal of the ROS-scavenging superoxide dismutase (SOD) does not increase oxidative damage to mtDNA.
source: In the same organism, removal of the ROS-scavenging superoxide dismutase (SOD) does not increase oxidative damage to mtDNA and has no apparent effect on lifespan (Doonan et al., 2008; Gruber et al., 2011; Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In C. elegans, removal of SOD has no apparent effect on lifespan.
source: In the same organism, removal of the ROS-scavenging superoxide dismutase (SOD) does not increase oxidative damage to mtDNA and has no apparent effect on lifespan (Doonan et al., 2008; Gruber et al., 2011; Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the fly, SOD knockouts have a decreased lifespan.
source: In the fly, SOD knockouts do have a decreased lifespan, but they do not accumulate mtDNA mutations more quickly than wildtype (Itsara et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In the fly, SOD knockouts do not accumulate mtDNA mutations more quickly than wildtype.
source: In the fly, SOD knockouts do have a decreased lifespan, but they do not accumulate mtDNA mutations more quickly than wildtype (Itsara et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A defect in the supra-molecular organisation of the ATP synthase results in aberrant cristae morphology in yeast and mouse mitochondria.
source: Recent analyses of yeast and mouse mitochondria show that a defect in the supra-molecular organisation of the ATP synthase results in aberrant cristae morphology (Davies et al., 2012; Mourier et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In aged cultures of Podospora anserina, the inner membrane vesiculates and ATP synthase dimers break down.
source: In aged cultures of the short-lived filamentous fungus Podospora anserina, the inner membrane strikingly vesiculates and ATP synthase dimers break down (Brust et al., 2010; Daum et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies of mouse liver by electron microscopy revealed anomalous cristae in a subpopulation of the organelles.
source: Previous studies of the ultrastructure of mitochondria in mouse liver by electron microscopy of thin plastic sections revealed anomalous cristae in a subpopulation of the organelles (Wilson and Franks, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mitochondria from aged D. melanogaster flight muscle were found to have cristae 'swirls' that were attributed to oxidative damage.
source: Mitochondria from aged D. melanogaster flight muscle were found to have cristae 'swirls' that were attributed to oxidative damage (Walker and Benzer, 2004), and mitochondria in aged Drosophila repleta heart muscle were enlarged (Sohal, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mitochondria in aged Drosophila repleta heart muscle were enlarged.
source: Mitochondria from aged D. melanogaster flight muscle were found to have cristae 'swirls' that were attributed to oxidative damage (Walker and Benzer, 2004), and mitochondria in aged Drosophila repleta heart muscle were enlarged (Sohal, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mitochondrial respiratory rates normalised to protein content were highest in heart mitochondria.
source: Mitochondrial respiratory rates normalised to protein content were found to be highest in heart mitochondria, ~2–3 fold lower in kidney and ~5 fold lower in liver (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Mitochondrial respiratory rates in kidney were ~2–3 fold lower than in heart.
source: Mitochondrial respiratory rates normalised to protein content were found to be highest in heart mitochondria, ~2–3 fold lower in kidney and ~5 fold lower in liver (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Mitochondrial respiratory rates in liver were ~5 fold lower than in heart.
source: Mitochondrial respiratory rates normalised to protein content were found to be highest in heart mitochondria, ~2–3 fold lower in kidney and ~5 fold lower in liver (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: There are no significant differences in respiratory rates between mitochondria isolated from 20-week-old and 80-week-old heart tissue.
source: In line with previous reports (Mulligan et al., 2014; Weindruch et al., 1980; Wilson et al., 1975), our investigation showed no significant differences in respiratory rates between mitochondria isolated from 20-week-old and 80-week-old heart tissue (Figure 1A), and no age-related change in the rate of ATP production was observed (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry data in Figure 1A and citations to previous research.

claim: No age-related change in the rate of ATP production was observed in heart mitochondria.
source: In line with previous reports (Mulligan et al., 2014; Weindruch et al., 1980; Wilson et al., 1975), our investigation showed no significant differences in respiratory rates between mitochondria isolated from 20-week-old and 80-week-old heart tissue (Figure 1A), and no age-related change in the rate of ATP production was observed (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP synthesis rate data in Figure 1C.

claim: Maximal activities of key mitochondrial enzymes remained unchanged with age in heart tissue.
source: Moreover, maximal activities of key mitochondrial enzymes remained unchanged (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity data in Figure 1E.

claim: No age-dependent increase in hydrogen peroxide release relative to the amount of oxygen consumed was observed in mitochondria isolated from heart, liver or kidney.
source: Surprisingly, no age-dependent increase in hydrogen peroxide release relative to the amount of oxygen consumed was observed in mitoch﻿ondria isolated from heart, liver or kidney (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by peroxide yield data in Figure 1B.

claim: There is a tendency towards lower levels of antioxidant enzymes in aged mice.
source: This revealed a tendency towards lower levels of antioxidant enzymes in aged mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from western blot data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Catalase activity was reduced by 30% in old mouse liver.
source: Catalase activity was reduced by 30% in old mouse liver (Figure 1F) and SOD activity was almost halved in old mouse kidney (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity data in Figure 1F.

claim: SOD activity was almost halved in old mouse kidney.
source: Catalase activity was reduced by 30% in old mouse liver (Figure 1F) and SOD activity was almost halved in old mouse kidney (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitochondria isolated from young mouse heart showed stacks of parallel, thin and flat lamellar cristae embedded in a dense matrix.
source: Mitochondria isolated from young mouse heart showed morphologies typical of tissues with a high energy demand. Stacks of parallel, thin and flat lamellar cristae were embedded in a dense matrix (Figure 2, left, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Crista junctions in young mouse heart mitochondria were circular (70%, average diameter 15 ± 2 nm) or slightly elongated (30%, 16 ± 1 × 29 ± 2 nm).
source: Crista junctions were circular (70%, average diameter 15 ± 2 nm) or slightly elongated (30%, 16 ± 1 × 29 ± 2 nm, dimensions ± standard deviations measured in the typical tomogram of Figure 2, top row, second from left).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from electron cryo-tomography data.

claim: Most cristae in young mouse heart mitochondria were branched and connected to the inter-membrane space by more than one junction.
source: Most cristae were branched and connected to the inter-membrane space by more than one junction.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations.

claim: In 20% of young mouse heart mitochondria examined, membranes of two or more neighbouring cristae were so closely appressed that there was almost no matrix between them.
source: In 20% of the mitochondria examined, membranes of two or more neighbouring cristae were so closely appressed that there was almost no matrix between them.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations.

claim: About 24% of mitochondria from aged heart tissue had some exceptionally wide cristae.
source: Comparing mitochondria from young and old mouse hearts indicated similar morphologies (Figure 2, right), except that about 24% of mitochondria from aged heart tissue had some exceptionally wide cristae (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The morphology of mitochondria isolated from mouse liver was conspicuously different from that of mouse heart.
source: The morphology of mitochondria isolated from mouse liver was conspicuously different from that of mouse heart (Figure 3, left; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Liver mitochondria cristae were more heterogeneous, less regular and not arranged in parallel stacks compared to heart mitochondria.
source: The cristae were more heterogeneous, less regular and not arranged in parallel stacks.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations of liver mitochondria.

claim: 32% of mitochondria from old mouse liver had conspicuous low-density compartments, or voids, in the centre of the organelle.
source: While the majority of mitochondria looked similar to those isolated from young mouse liver, 32% (n = 31) had conspicuous low-density compartments, or voids, in the centre of the organelle (Figure 3, right, Video 3; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The voids in old liver mitochondria accounted on average for 22% of the total cristae surface in three segmented mitochondria.
source: In three segmented mitochondria, the voids accounted on average for 22% of the total cristae surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electron cryo-tomography data.

claim: The voids in old liver mitochondria occupied on average 6% of the total mitochondrial volume in three segmented organelles.
source: In the three segmented organelles, the voids occupied on average 6% of the total mitochondrial volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of electron cryo-tomography data.

claim: The voids in old liver mitochondria were not internal vesicles, but were connected to the inter-membrane space via apertures of varying size.
source: The voids were not internal vesicles, but were connected to the inter-membrane space via apertures of varying size.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations.

claim: 18% of kidney mitochondria from old mice had the characteristic morphology described for apoptotic cells.
source: 18% of kidney mitochondria from old mice and 12% from young mice had the characteristic morphology described for apoptotic cells (Scorrano et al., 2002; Sun et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data and citations to previous research on apoptotic mitochondria.

claim: 12% of kidney mitochondria from young mice had the characteristic morphology described for apoptotic cells.
source: 18% of kidney mitochondria from old mice and 12% from young mice had the characteristic morphology described for apoptotic cells (Scorrano et al., 2002; Sun et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data and citations to previous research on apoptotic mitochondria.

claim: A minor respiratory defect was found under phosphorylating and uncoupling conditions in heart from mtDNA mutator mice.
source: A minor respiratory defect was found under phosphorylating and uncoupling conditions in heart from mtDNA mutator mice (Figure 5A), consistent with previous observations (Trifunovic et al., 2004, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry data in Figure 5A and citations to previous research.

claim: 40% of heart mitochondria from mtDNA mutator mice had ellipsoidal peripheral voids connected to the cristae or the inter-membrane space that were delineated by a double membrane.
source: The morphology of heart mitochondria from the mtDNA mutator mice resembled wildtype heart mitochondria, except for a high incidence (40%) of ellipsoidal peripheral voids connected to the cristae or the inter-membrane space that were delineated by a double membrane (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 40% of liver mitochondria from mutator mice had low-density central voids.
source: Mitochondria isolated from mtDNA mutator mouse liver showed the same central low-density voids (Figure 5C) as liver mitochondria from old wild-type mice (Figure 3), but at greater prevalence (40%; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data shown in Figure 5C and Table 1.

claim: The flies showed standard sigmoidal survival curves, with a mean lifespan of 69.5 days and a maximum lifespan of 78.5 days.
source: The flies showed standard sigmoidal survival curves, with a mean lifespan of 69.5 days and a maximum lifespan of 78.5 days (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Life span correlated with climbing ability in flies.
source: Life span correlated with climbing ability, as reported previously (Rhodenizer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A and citation to previous research.

claim: Climbing ability in flies remained constant for 25 days and then dropped rapidly.
source: Climbing ability remained constant for 25 days and then dropped rapidly (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by climbing ability data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The respiration rate in old flies decreased by up to 60%.
source: The respiration rate in old flies decreased by up to 60% (Figure 6B), and the peroxide yield increased by 40–100% (Figure 6C), indicating that mitochondrial function is severely compromised, confirming an earlier report (Ferguson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry data in Figure 6B and citation to previous research.

claim: The peroxide yield in old flies increased by 40–100%.
source: The respiration rate in old flies decreased by up to 60% (Figure 6B), and the peroxide yield increased by 40–100% (Figure 6C), indicating that mitochondrial function is severely compromised, confirming an earlier report (Ferguson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by peroxide yield data in Figure 6C and citation to previous research.

claim: Mitochondria from young flies had a dense matrix and thin, lamellar, mostly parallel cristae.
source: Mitochondria from young flies (n = 29; Figure 6D, Video 4) looked similar to those from mouse heart, with a dense matrix and thin, lamellar, mostly parallel cristae.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All cristae in young fly mitochondria had ridges indicative of ATP synthase dimer rows.
source: All cristae had ridges indicative of ATP synthase dimer rows (Davies et al., 2011; Strauss et al., 2008) and several junctions to the intermembrane space.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations and citations to previous research.

claim: Wide cristae were observed in 10% of mitochondria from young flies.
source: Wide cristae were observed in 10% of the mitochondria, similar to mouse heart.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations.

claim: A small subpopulation of mitochondria (10%) from young flies was unusually elongated (axial ratio above 3:1).
source: A small subpopulation of mitochondria (10%) was unusually elongated (axial ratio above 3:1) but looked otherwise normal.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations.

claim: The structure of mitochondria from old D. melanogaster was heterogeneous.
source: By contrast, the structure of mitochondria from old D. melanogaster (n = 39) was heterogeneous (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Approximately 75% of mitochondria from old flies had normal, well-developed cristae.
source: Approximately 75% of mitochondria had normal, well-developed cristae, although in 15% the cristae were wider (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations.

claim: In 25% of old fly mitochondria, the inner membrane assumed a variety of non-standard shapes.
source: In the remaining 25% of old fly mitochondria, the inner membrane assumed a variety of non-standard shapes.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations.

claim: Several old fly mitochondria that were identified as mitochondria by their characteristic double membrane and dense matrix appeared to lack cristae entirely.
source: Several organelles that were identified as mitochondria by their characteristic double membrane and dense matrix appeared to lack cristae entirely (Figure 6E, top right) or the cristae were minimally developed (10%).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There is a clear correlation between OXPHOS capacity and the number of inner membrane cristae per unit volume.
source: We found a clear correlation between OXPHOS capacity and the number of inner membrane cristae per unit volume.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparative data on respiratory rates and cristae density across different tissues.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration was highest in mouse heart and young fly mitochondria, which were entirely filled with closely stacked, parallel cristae.
source: Mitochondrial respiration was highest in mouse heart and young fly mitochondria, which were entirely filled with closely stacked, parallel cristae.
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry and electron cryo-tomography data.

claim: Cristae fenestration is a morphological characteristic of tissues with high energy demand.
source: In mouse heart and young fly mitochondria, we frequently observed cristae fenestration, which is a morphological characteristic of tissues with high energy demand (Slautterback, 1965; Smith, 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations and citations to previous research.

claim: Fenestration increases the total length of cristae ridges that harbour the ATP synthase, and hence the potential for ATP production.
source: Fenestration increases the total length of cristae ridges that harbour the ATP synthase, and hence the potential for ATP production.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the structural organization of ATP synthase at cristae ridges.

claim: A significant proportion of kidney mitochondria from both young and old mice had a morphology typical of apoptotic cells.
source: Remarkably, a significant proportion of kidney mitochondria from both young and old mice had a morphology typical of apoptotic cells (Scorrano et al., 2002; Sun et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data and citations to previous research on apoptotic mitochondria.

claim: The apoptotic morphology of kidney mitochondria correlates well with the recently reported continuous turnover and short lifespan of kidney cells of about 30–60 days.
source: This correlates well with the recently reported continuous turnover and short lifespan of kidney cells of about 30–60 days (Rinkevich et al., 2014), compared to the 200–400 day lifespan of rat hepatic cells (Macdonald, 1961) and the very low turnover rates for cardiomyocytes of 1.3–4% per year (Malliaras et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on correlation with cited research on cell turnover rates.

claim: The peroxide yield correlated inversely with respiratory activity and was highest in mouse liver and lowest in mouse heart.
source: The peroxide yield correlated inversely with respiratory activity and was highest in mouse liver and lowest in mouse heart, suggesting that liver mitochondria may be affected by oxidative damage more severely than mitochondria from cardiac tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Figure 1A and 1B showing respiratory rates and peroxide yields.

claim: Liver mitochondria may be affected by oxidative damage more severely than mitochondria from cardiac tissue.
source: The peroxide yield correlated inversely with respiratory activity and was highest in mouse liver and lowest in mouse heart, suggesting that liver mitochondria may be affected by oxidative damage more severely than mitochondria from cardiac tissue.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the inverse correlation between respiratory activity and peroxide yield.

claim: Levels of mitochondrial respiration, respiratory chain activity, hydrogen peroxide production or steady-state levels of antioxidant enzymes did not vary greatly with age in mice.
source: Unexpectedly, levels of mitochondrial respiration, respiratory chain activity, hydrogen peroxide production or steady-state levels of antioxidant enzymes did not vary greatly with age, indicating moderate changes at most in respiratory rates and hydrogen peroxide yield in ageing mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Figure 1.

claim: The findings on mouse mitochondrial function contravene the free-radical theory of ageing.
source: This contravenes the free-radical theory of ageing, which postulates a major age-related increase in ROS production and respiratory defects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of age-related changes in ROS production and respiratory function.

claim: The morphology of mouse heart mitochondria did not change much with age.
source: In line with our results on mitochondrial function, the morphology of mouse heart mitochondria did not change much with age.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data from Figure 2.

claim: One out of four mitochondria from old mouse livers had a striking, age-specific phenotype characterized by a central matrix void.
source: By contrast, one out of four mitochondria from old mouse livers had a striking, age-specific phenotype characterized by a central matrix void.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data from Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The same central void feature was found in mitochondria of mtDNA mutator mouse livers, where it was considerably more prevalent.
source: We found the same feature in mitochondria of mtDNA mutator mouse livers, where it was considerably more prevalent.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data from Figure 5C and Table 1.

claim: The lack of sharp cristae ridges and crista junctions in the void membranes suggests that these membranes do not contain ATP synthase dimers.
source: The lack of sharp cristae ridges and crista junctions in the void membranes suggests that these mebranes do not contain ATP synthase dimers and hence do not contribute to oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known structural organization of ATP synthase dimers at cristae ridges.

claim: Void membranes do not contribute to oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The lack of sharp cristae ridges and crista junctions in the void membranes suggests that these mebranes do not contain ATP synthase dimers and hence do not contribute to oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of ATP synthase dimers in void membranes.

claim: If the majority of mitochondria are normal, they can apparently compensate for a loss of inner membrane area available for oxidative phosphorylation in 25% of the total population.
source: The fact that mitochondria with these central voids have otherwise normal cristae may explain why no age-related reduction in overall respiratory activity was evident. If the majority of mitochondria are normal, they can apparently compensate for a loss of inner membrane area available for oxidative phosphorylation in 25% of the total population.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the lack of overall respiratory decline despite structural abnormalities in a subpopulation.

claim: Similar ring- or cup-shaped mitochondria with central cavities have been reported and ascribed to the effects of drugs, toxins or oxidative damage.
source: Similar ring- or cup-shaped mitochondria with central cavities have been reported (Ghadially, 1988) and ascribed to the effects of drugs, toxins (David and Kettler, 1961; Stephens and Bils, 1965) or oxidative damage (Ding et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The central voids in old liver mitochondria may result from oxidative damage.
source: Although the cavities found in these earlier studies were lined by both the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes, the central voids described here may likewise result from such damage, as damage to mtDNA is known to accumulate in liver tissues (Barazzoni et al., 2000; Yen et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on previous reports and known mtDNA damage accumulation in liver.

claim: Damage to mtDNA is known to accumulate in liver tissues.
source: Although the cavities found in these earlier studies were lined by both the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes, the central voids described here may likewise result from such damage, as damage to mtDNA is known to accumulate in liver tissues (Barazzoni et al., 2000; Yen et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: If denatured respiratory chain complexes are cleared from the membrane, the lipids left behind would be expected to form featureless membrane regions expanding into the matrix interior.
source: If denatured respiratory chain complexes are cleared from the membrane, the lipids left behind would be expected to form such featureless membrane regions expanding into the matrix interior.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the formation of voids.

claim: The matrix granules found in old liver and kidney mitochondria may consist at least in part of denatured respiratory chain complexes.
source: The matrix granules that we found in old liver and kidney mitochondria may consist at least in part of denatured respiratory chain complexes, consistent with their absence from old heart mitochondria, in which we did not observe matrix granules.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the distribution of granules and previous research.

claim: Matrix granules contain complex IV subunits in addition to lipids, glycoproteins and calcium.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that these granules contain complex IV subunits (Hertsens et al., 1986) in addition to lipids, glycoproteins and calcium (Ghadially, 2001; Jacob et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in the membrane structure of mouse mitochondria were organ-dependent.
source: Interestingly, changes in the membrane structure of mouse mitochondria were organ-dependent, in a way that suggests different degrees of resilience against ageing.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from heart, liver, and kidney mitochondria.

claim: Mouse cardiac mitochondria appeared to be protected most effectively from oxidative damage.
source: Mouse cardiac mitochondria showed the highest respiratory rates but appeared to be protected most effectively from oxidative damage, as indicated by their low and unchanged peroxide yield.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data on respiratory rates and peroxide yields.

claim: The findings on mouse cardiac mitochondria contradict the classical free-radical theory.
source: Again, these findings contradict the classical free-radical theory, which would predict that cardiomyocytes with their high density of highly active mitochondria produce more ROS and thus age faster (Stuart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the contradiction between observed data and theoretical predictions.

claim: An analysis of DNA methylation has shown that heart tissue ages more slowly than would be predicted chronologically.
source: An analysis of DNA methylation has shown that heart tissue ages more slowly than would be predicted chronologically (Horvath, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mitochondria in vital organs with slow regeneration, such as the heart, are protected from damage more effectively than mitochondria in other organs.
source: This observation is in line with our findings, which thus imply that mitochondria in vital organs with slow regeneration, such as the heart, are protected from damage more effectively than mitochondria in other organs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in mitochondrial ageing across tissues.

claim: The protective effect on heart mitochondria may be genetically controlled through the expression levels of superoxide dismutase or catalase.
source: The effect may be genetically controlled through the expression levels of superoxide dismutase or catalase.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of protection.

claim: Overexpression of catalase targeted to mitochondria has been shown to attenuate ageing effects in the murine heart.
source: Overexpression of catalase targeted to mitochondria has been shown to attenuate ageing effects in the murine heart (Dai et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: About half of the mitochondria from old flies had lost the standard organization of the inner membrane into boundary membranes with well-developed cristae and crista junctions.
source: About half of the mitochondria from old flies had lost the standard organization of the inner membrane into boundary membranes with well-developed cristae and crista junctions.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography data from Figure 6E.

claim: Many old fly mitochondria had round or concentric cristae that lacked sharp ridges.
source: Many had round or concentric cristae that lacked sharp ridges.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron cryo-tomography observations.

claim: Measurements of respiratory activity in old fly mitochondria indicated that oxygen uptake was decreased by a factor of almost two.
source: Measurements of respiratory activity in old fly mitochondria indicated that oxygen uptake was decreased by a factor of almost two and peroxide yield was increased by more than 50%, in line with increased mitochondrial H2O2 production in live ageing Drosophila (Cochemé et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by respirometry data from Figure 6B and citation to previous research.

claim: Peroxide yield in old fly mitochondria was increased by more than 50%.
source: Measurements of respiratory activity in old fly mitochondria indicated that oxygen uptake was decreased by a factor of almost two and peroxide yield was increased by more than 50%, in line with increased mitochondrial H2O2 production in live ageing Drosophila (Cochemé et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by peroxide yield data from Figure 6C and citation to previous research.

claim: About 50% of the old fly mitochondria are inactive.
source: These results suggest strongly that about 50% of the old fly mitochondria are inactive, consistent with the observation that about 25% of the mitochondria in old flies lack normal cristae or crista junctions and that an additional 18% deviate from the standard morphology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between structural abnormalities and functional decline.

claim: A drastic breakdown of mitochondrial structure and function would result in the death of the organism within a short period.
source: Such a drastic breakdown of mitochondrial structure and function would result in the death of the organism within a short period.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the critical role of mitochondria in cellular function.

claim: P. anserina has an average lifespan of only 18 days, three times shorter than D. melanogaster, and almost 50 times shorter than mouse.
source: P. anserina has an average lifespan of only 18 days, three times shorter than D. melanogaster, and almost 50 times shorter than mouse.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the lifespans of these model organisms.

claim: Morphological changes in P. anserina mitochondria were both more homogenous and more extreme than those in fruit flies, affecting about 80% of organelles from senescent populations.
source: Morphological changes in P. anserina mitochondria were both more homogenous and more extreme than those in fruit flies, affecting about 80% of organelles from senescent populations (Brust et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Cryo-ET of aged P. anserina mitochondria indicated that the cristae had receded into the inner boundary membrane and that ATP synthase dimers dissociated into monomers.
source: Cryo-ET of aged P. anserina mitochondria or inner membrane vesicles indicated that the cristae had receded into the inner boundary membrane and that ATP synthase dimers dissociated into monomers (Daum et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Old P. anserina mitochondria resembled the quasi-apoptotic subpopulation in mouse kidney.
source: In terms of inner membrane morphology, old P. anserina mitochondria resembled the quasi-apoptotic subpopulation in mouse kidney, the tissue with the highest turnover rate in our study, suggesting similar mechanisms of programmed ageing.
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological similarities.

claim: The higher proportion of functional mitochondria in old flies indicates that the decline is less complete and slower than that in P. anserina.
source: On the one hand, the higher proportion of functional mitochondria in old flies indicates that the decline is less complete and slower than that in P. anserina.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative data.

claim: Mitochondrial decline is much more rapid in D. melanogaster than in mouse.
source: On the other hand, it is much more rapid in D. melanogaster than in mouse, suggesting a link between the complexity of an organism and the rate of ageing.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative data.

claim: There is a link between the complexity of an organism and the rate of ageing.
source: On the other hand, it is much more rapid in D. melanogaster than in mouse, suggesting a link between the complexity of an organism and the rate of ageing.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparative observations.

claim: The increasing complexity of organisms goes along with an increasingly complex ageing process.
source: The increasing complexity of organisms goes along with an increasingly complex ageing process.
evidence: This is a general inference based on the comparative data from different organisms.

claim: For P. anserina, a straightforward correspondence between age, mitochondrial ultrastructure and organization of the mitochondrial ATP synthase has been shown.
source: For the primitive multicellular eukaryote P. anserina, a straightforward correspondence between age, mitochondrial ultrastructure and organization of the mitochondrial ATP synthase has been shown (Brust et al., 2010; Daum et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Drosophila, a link between inner membrane morphology and functionality is established, which correlates closely with age and agility.
source: In Drosophila, we now establish a link between inner membrane morphology and functionality, which correlates closely with age and agility.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data on structure, function, and climbing ability.

claim: In mouse, the relationship between inner membrane ultrastructure, function and age is less clear-cut and evidently tissue-dependent.
source: In mouse, the relationship between inner membrane ultrastructure, function and age is less clear-cut and evidently tissue-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative data from different mouse tissues.

claim: A quarter of liver mitochondria display a severe, age-related phenotype that does not seem to result in an overall reduction of oxidative phosphorylation.
source: While mouse heart mitochondria show little if any change with age, a quarter of liver mitochondria display a severe, age-related phenotype that does not seem to result in an overall reduction of oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural and functional data from liver mitochondria.

claim: The data indicate major differences in how ageing relates to mitochondrial morphology and function in metazoans.
source: Our data thus indicate major differences in how ageing relates to mitochondrial morphology and function in metazoans.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the comparative data.

claim: In mouse, there is no evidence of age-related progressive impairment of the oxidative phosphorylation system.
source: In mouse, we find no evidence of age-related progressive impairment of the oxidative phosphorylation system or increase of mitochondrial H2O2 production, whereas both effects are evident in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional data from mouse mitochondria.

claim: In mouse, there is no evidence of age-related increase of mitochondrial H2O2 production.
source: In mouse, we find no evidence of age-related progressive impairment of the oxidative phosphorylation system or increase of mitochondrial H2O2 production, whereas both effects are evident in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by the peroxide yield data from mouse mitochondria.

claim: Both impairment of the oxidative phosphorylation system and increase of mitochondrial H2O2 production are evident in Drosophila.
source: In mouse, we find no evidence of age-related progressive impairment of the oxidative phosphorylation system or increase of mitochondrial H2O2 production, whereas both effects are evident in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional data from Drosophila mitochondria.
